newsitem.title: USA: U.S. voters consider record $15 billion of bonds.
newsitem.headline: U.S. voters consider record $15 billion of bonds.

text.p: Americans on Tuesday will vote on $15.5 billion of municipal bond issues -- the largest slate of bond issues ever -- to finance everything from roads and bridges to clean water programmes, harbour dredging and schools.
Analysts said that voter optimism about the economy and the pressing need of almost $1 trillion of infrastructure projects could mean passage of many of the bonds.
"It's absolutely an ideal setting for passing referenda like we've got," said Robert Chamberlin, senior vice president of research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
There's a direct correlation between economic conditions and the approval rating, Chamberlin said.

During California's recession in the early 1990s, for instance, only about 40 percent of that state's ballots were approved. This time around, with the state in an economic rebound, California voters are expected to approve a bevy of bond issues in the polls.

When the U.S. economy was steaming ahead in 1995, 85 percent of the $7 billion of bonds across the nation were approved. But a year earlier, when growth was more uneven, only 66 percent of the $10 billion of bonds around the country were approved.
George Leung, a vice president with Moody's Investors Service, a major rating agency, said schools need the most financing.
"It's the greatest area of need," Leung said. "As to whether or not they get approved depends on the area in question."

"I think the mood overall is one in which there is a greater degree of conservatism and efficiency in government that the voters are demanding," he said. "Whether that translates into rejection of bond referendums or other initiatives really depends on the states or locales in question."
Over 50 percent of the dollar volume of bonds are in three states: California, New York and North Carolina.

California, one of the country's most prolific bond issuers, has the bulk of the bond ballot issues and also the largest single bond ballot issue: a $2 billion Los Angeles Unified School District, Calif., school bond proposal.
North Carolina voters will vote for almost $3 billion of general obligation bonds for schools and highways.

New York State voters will decide on a massive $1.75 billion New York Clean Water, Clean Air Bond Act. If approved, general obligation bond sales would fund a variety of environmental projects throughout the state. New York voters appear to favour the measure, according to polls.
